title: SpacetimeDB + AI-Generated Assets: Open-Source 2D Survival Game
author: MetalHorse233
selftext:
I’ve been prototyping a 2D multiplayer survival game called Broth and Bullets and wanted to share how it’s built and what I’ve learned so far.

Stack: React + TypeScript frontend, SpacetimeDB for authoritative multiplayer (no separate game server). The whole thing is open source. SpacetimeDB keeps game logic in the database, so reducers run server-side and clients subscribe to state over WebSocket.

AI usage: Most art is AI-generated: terrain, props, UI, background tiles, etc. The only non-AI assets are the main character spritesheets and a few hostile NPCs. Fast for iteration but the style is inconsistent, so I’m planning a Kickstarter to hire pixel artists for a full polish pass.

Costs: Production on SpacetimeDB Maincloud was around $200/month. I’m trying to lower that by tuning reducers (e.g. with newer SOTA models) and reducing compute-heavy logic. I also pre-purchased SpacetimeDB credits at a heavy discount when they launched, so I’m effectively paying about $20/month right now. That gives roughly a year of runway before I’ll need to think about monetization.

Open source: The repo is public on GitHub licensed under Apache 2.0 so you can clone it and use the code for your own projects but cant use the story/storyline etc. If you’re curious about the SpacetimeDB setup, multiplayer architecture, or how AI assets fit into a real-time game, you can dig into the code directly.

Live build: A production build is live and playable. If you want the link, I can share it in a follow-up so this doesn’t look like a drive-by promotion.

Happy to answer questions about SpacetimeDB, multiplayer architecture, AI asset pipelines, or anything else related to the project.

replies.author: MetalHorse233
replies.body:
You can check out the repo here:  
[https://github.com/SeloSlav/2d-multiplayer-survival-mmorpg](https://github.com/SeloSlav/2d-multiplayer-survival-mmorpg)

Just clone it locally with `git clone` and follow the quick install steps in the README to get the game running. Once it’s up, you can import the project into Cursor and start editing with AI, or open it in VS Code with Claude Code or whatever setup you prefer.

If you’re curious what originally got me interested in using SpacetimeDB, take a look at this project as well:  
[https://github.com/majidmanzarpour/vibe-coding-starter-pack-3d-multiplayer](https://github.com/majidmanzarpour/vibe-coding-starter-pack-3d-multiplayer)

replies.author: MetalHorse233
replies.body: 😂 Not quite. The costs shouldn’t scale linearly with player count given the way the system’s designed. A large portion of the load comes from environment respawn schedulers and baseline infrastructure, so it behaves more like a fixed base cost than a pure per-player subscription curve.

comments.author: -goldenboi69-
comments.body: How much are all the api calls (to the ai apis) costing you per month so far,? And I mean "in game", not the cost for vibing it.

replies.author: MetalHorse233
replies.body: I couldn’t say for sure yet since I haven’t marketed the game much, but I expect the impact to be negligible. The AI calls are lightweight and mostly text-only. Models like GPT-4o mini and Grok-1.5 Mini are used for recipe generation and assistant responses, so the per-user inference cost should stay very low.

replies.author: Chinoman10
replies.body:
If you use open-source models on Groq or Cerebras, not only can you get *MUCH* faster outputs but also orders of magnitude lower costs (I run thousands of prompts on a daily basis and pay just a few dollars at the end of the month consistently).
As long as you already have a RAG system in place to ground their answers on true knowledge (and not hallucinated), you're gold 👌

replies.author: MetalHorse233
replies.body:
I paid a pixel artist to handle the main character spritesheets. I haven’t found anything yet that can reliably generate character tilesets in a consistent custom style. I was able to get the animals working somewhat with the prompt below, but in my opinion they still came out a bit janky.

-----

Subject: black tundra wolf

Style:
Modern AAA pixel art (Sea of Stars quality).
Clean, intentional pixel clusters.
Clear, consistent black outlines.
Soft internal shading derived from the reference image.
Naturalistic proportions (not cute, not chibi).

Palette:
Colors sampled and simplified from the reference image.
Preserve the reference material feel.

OUTPUT FORMAT

Output a single flattened PNG image

No simulated transparency (no checkerboard or patterns)

No per-frame background rectangles

All non-subject pixels must be one single flat magenta background color

CANVAS & GRID (ABSOLUTE)

Canvas: 256 × 256 pixels

Grid: 4 rows × 4 columns (exactly 16 sprites)

Cell size: 64 × 64 pixels

No borders, grid lines, padding, or gutters

Do not omit, merge, or add frames

CAMERA & FACING (CRITICAL)

Each row uses a locked camera orientation.
The subject’s body and head orientation must not rotate within a row.

Row 1: Facing DOWN (South)

Row 2: Facing RIGHT (East)

Row 3: Facing LEFT (West)

Row 4: Facing UP (North)

Each direction must be a true redraw, not a mirror.
No diagonal angles, no partial rotation, no perspective drift.

ANIMATION (LOCOMOTION ONLY)

4 frames per row.

The subject stays centered in its 64×64 cell

The facing direction remains identical across all 4 frames

Motion is created only by limb movement and body weight shift

Frame progression:

Contact pose

Weight shift forward

Opposite contact

Neutral return

No turning, no rotation, no camera change.

ALIGNMENT

Ground-align all sprites within the same row

No body part may leave its 64×64 cell

Scale down if needed, never crop

RENDERING RULES

No text, UI, props, or effects

No shadows cast onto the background

Consistent lighting across all frames

Consistent outline thickness
